newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Chretien threatened by Conservative surge.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Chretien threatened by Conservative surge.

text.p: Conservative Party leader Jean Charest, 38, has suddenly emerged as a young, articulate threat to 63-year-old Liberal Prime Minister Jean Chretien in Canada's election campaign.
Charest's growing prominence has thrown the race wide open in Quebec and Atlantic Canada, though he has yet to catch fire in the rest of the country.

Many detest the Conservatives because of memories of former prime minister Brian Mulroney who stepped down in 1993, and polls suggested Charest was unlikely to lead them back to power a mere 3-1/2 years after near annihilation by voters.

But voters reckoned he easily outperformed his rivals in debates last week, attracting the attention especially of residents of French-speaking Quebec, where the question of whether Canada should remain united is critical.

"I think he's the one that seems to be the most ardent and genuine and enthusiastic about the unity issue," Cornell Berwald, a 71-year-old retired school principal from the Quebec town of Val Morin, said in a phone interview.
"I think he's pulling in an awful lot of votes like that."
Charest won the affection of many Canadians when he took a prominent role in pleading eloquently for his country to stand united during a 1995 referendum on Quebec sovereignty.

Chretien, a generation older and more worn-looking than Charest, took flak for nearly losing the referendum. Critics charged he had neither a Plan A to keep Quebec in nor a Plan B to deal with a vote to separate.
The most recent polls put the Conservatives at between 15 and 27 points behind the Liberals nationally, but closer in Quebec, which will have 75 out of the 301 seats in the new Parliament.

A poll in the Globe and Mail even put the Conservatives ahead of both the Liberals and the separatist Bloc Quebecois in Quebec for the first time since the 1993 election, possibly pointing to the downfall of the Bloc but also limiting Liberal hopes for recovery there.
As in the case of U.S. presidential candidate Bob Dole in 1996, age seemed to play an underlying role, even if direct references were rare.
Reporter Normand Rheaume asked Chretien in a debate on Quebec on Sunday whether he was "the man of the hour" or if after 34 years in politics he had become part of the problem.

"I'd like to see a little fresh thought perhaps, and perhaps somebody younger who has a little more get-up-and-go," said voter Ian Naismith, 65, a retired quality assurance manager from Dundas, Ontario, who was leaning toward Charest.

Charest was first elected to Parliament in 1984 at age 26. Two years later he became the youngest person to serve in a Canadian cabinet, rising in 1993 to be appointed deputy prime minister for a few months before federal elections.

He was one of only two Conservatives to survive the 1993 election and, elected Conservative leader shortly afterward, spent the following years tirelessly criss-crossing Canada to rebuild the Tory fortunes.
But he remained haunted by the ghost of Mulroney, who was initially popular but soon became hated for perceived arrogance, corruption and failure to tackle high deficits and unemployment.

"He's running for the wrong party right now, because Brian Mulroney left the Conservatives in so big a mess it's hard to make people start to believe in the party," said Karl Horvaph, a British Columbian who supports the right-wing Reform Party.

Some of the factors that work in his favour in Quebec -- being a fluently bilingual Quebecker who wants to entrench the province's "distinctiveness" in the constitution -- have worked against him in Ontario and the West, home to Reform.
In one debate, Reform leader Preston Manning scorned the squabbling between three Quebec politicians -- Chretien, Charest and the Bloc's Gilles Duceppe.

After hammering hard on tax cuts in the first two weeks of the campaign, Charest based much of his appeal in the last week on character and leadership, prompting Manning to charge that both Charest and Chretien were offering only "mush."

Separatist Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard echoed this: "If the marketing experts in Ottawa could reinvent Jean Chretien, they would, they would have him like Jean Charest. He is the closest thing to political cloning you can get."

But one of Charest's biggest problems is that he is having to scrap with Reform for the right-wing vote west of Quebec. In the treasure chest of Ontario, with more than a third of the seats, polls so far point to a near sweep by the Liberals.
